title: The Back-to-Back Loan: Patti to Voghera, a Bank Emptied and a Liquidator Killed
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Patti, the wreath-maker's first son
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani DBI: 'Nacque l'8 maggio 1920 a Patti (Messina), figlio primogenito di Antonino e di Maria Castelnuovo.' Coordinate is the comune centre per OSM/Nominatim (Patti, Messina, Sicilia, 98066); three separate research passes produced three different and all incorrect Patti coordinates, none of which is used here.
stops.campa: In Patti, on the Tyrrhenian coast of the province of Messina, Antonino Sindona sells flowers, and his steadiest trade is in funeral wreaths. His first son is born on the eighth of May, 1920, to him and to Maria Castelnuovo. The family is of modest means. The town keeps its saint's bones in the cathedral and its money in the ground, and the boy born here will spend his working life moving other people's money out of the ground and across borders where no court can follow it. He is baptized Michele.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, voce 'Michele Sindona'
The nickname 'lo squalo di Patti', widely repeated in the Italian press but not traced to any encyclopedic source in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'
it.wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona' (father a florist specialising in funeral wreaths)

stops.name: Messina, the boy in the offices
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance, reconstructed as to date. it.wikipedia states he worked from the age of fourteen as typist, accounting assistant and employee of the Messina tax office; age fourteen puts the start in 1934. The month and day are an ordering device and carry no authority. An earlier pass dated this period 'early 1940s', which is too late by most of a decade.
stops.campa: He is fourteen when he begins working: typist, then assistant in accounts, then a clerk in the Messina tax office. He learns the shape of an Italian balance sheet from the side that inspects it, which is the side that knows where a balance sheet can be made to lie. Messina is still a rebuilt city, thrown up over the rubble left by the earthquake of 1908, which flattened it and killed most of the people in it. He comes in from Patti along the coast, works the day, and reads at night.
suggested_refs: The Ufficio imposte of Messina, his first employer inside the Italian fiscal machinery

stops.name: Messina, the law degree
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Britannica and Treccani both give 1942 for the law degree from the University of Messina); no source fetched in this pass gives the month or day, so the date defaults to 01-01.
stops.campa: He takes his degree in law from the University of Messina in 1942, in the third year of a war that is going badly for Italy and that will shortly arrive on this island. He has already spent eight years inside the machinery of tax assessment, and the law he now holds a diploma in is that same machinery read from the other end. No source says how he did in the examinations. What the record fixes is the field he goes into: never criminal law, never the courts, but the law of what a company owns and what it can be said to owe. The degree is dated 1942, and the day and the month were not written down.
suggested_refs: Facoltà di Giurisprudenza, Università degli Studi di Messina, graduating class of 1942
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Messina, the Allied officers and the trucks
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance and year, reconstructed as to month. it.wikipedia dates the smuggling fortune to 1943, immediately after the Allied landing in Sicily, and names AMGOT officers as counterparties alongside Mafia contacts. An earlier pass carried 1946 for this, apparently back-formed from the Milan move; Messina fell in August 1943 and the month is set from that, not from a source.
stops.campa: The Allies land in Sicily in July and take Messina in August. The Allied Military Government arrives with fuel, papers and permits, and Sicily arrives with everything the Allied Military Government wants moved. Sindona is twenty-three and works the seam: food and goods carried on the black market, with AMGOT officers on one side of the transaction and Mafia contacts on the other. Neither side can deal with the other directly. He stands between them, and takes a share of everything that passes, and this is the fortune he goes north with.
suggested_refs: Allied Military Government of Occupied Territory, Sicily 1943-1944, permit and requisition records

stops.name: Sicily, marriage to Caterina Cilio
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date by Britannica's biography; the place is given only as Sicily by the sources fetched, so the pin defaults to his birthplace and should not be read as an attested wedding site.
stops.campa: On the fourth of September, 1944, with the war still grinding north up the peninsula and Sicily behind the front, he marries Caterina Cilio. Three children will follow: Maria Elisa, Nino, Marco. The marriage lasts the whole of his life, through Milan and the Vatican and New York and the staged kidnapping and the maximum-security wing at Voghera, and Caterina is still his wife on the morning he carries his coffee into a prison bathroom. Of her the record kept by his prosecutors and his biographers says almost nothing else.
suggested_refs: Britannica, 'Michele Sindona', on the marriage and the three children

stops.name: Milan, the law office opens
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both Britannica and Treccani; Treccani specifies the summer of 1946, which fixes the month only loosely. Coordinate is the Milan city pin, not a street address: no source fetched gives the location of the first office.
stops.campa: He goes north in 1946, to a city bombed flat through its centre and rebuilding at speed, and opens a law office. What he sells is not litigation but arithmetic: tax advice to Lombard industrialists whose money is moving faster than the state can count it. He is discreet and he is available, and the work comes to him. Within a decade the men who own northern Italy's factories know his name; within two, so does the Institute for the Works of Religion. Treccani puts the opening of the office in the summer of 1946. No source fetched gives the street.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, on the Milanese consulting practice
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Vaduz, Fasco AG at the top of the pyramid
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia ('circa 1950'); no month or day in any source fetched, so the date defaults to 01-01. The back-to-back technique is described in en.wikipedia's account of the Fasco structure.
stops.campa: At thirty he founds Fasco AG in Liechtenstein, a principality of eleven thousand people that asks holding companies no questions. Fasco sits at the top of the pyramid for the next twenty-five years, and every bank he ever buys is bought through it. With it comes the technique he becomes known for, the back-to-back loan: one of his banks lends to a shell company, the shell lends the money back, and the same funds show as an asset in two places at once. He is rarely in Vaduz himself. The company has an address there, which is all Liechtenstein asks of it.
suggested_refs: Fasco AG / Fasco International, the Liechtenstein holding vehicle for every subsequent acquisition

stops.name: Via Albricci, the American in the attic
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance by it.wikipedia, which places Joe Adonis's exile apartment in the attic on Via Albricci within Sindona's Milanese circle; the decade is 'the 1950s' and the date here is a mid-decade ordering device only. Coordinate is the street, unverified against a building number.
stops.campa: In an attic on Via Albricci lives Joe Adonis, deported from the United States and serving his exile in Milan, still wired to everything he was wired to in New York. Sindona's Milan is a small city and its circles overlap: the tax adviser to industrialists and the exiled mobster move through the same rooms. No court ever fixed a date on which the lawyer crossed over, and it.wikipedia puts the two of them in the same circle without saying more than that. What is on the record is the address, the decade, and the proximity.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Joe Adonis', on the Milan years of the deportation

stops.name: Milan, presented to Montini
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by it.wikipedia: Sindona meets Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini in 1954 through Monsignor Amleto Tondini. Month and day unrecorded. An earlier pass dated the Vatican relationship vaguely to 'the 1960s', which conflates this introduction with the IOR business that only begins in 1968-69. Montini was made Archbishop of Milan in 1954, which is why the stop is pinned here rather than in Rome; no source names the room.
stops.campa: Monsignor Amleto Tondini brings him to Giovanni Battista Montini, newly made Archbishop of Milan, who will be Pope Paul VI in nine years. Until now he is a Sicilian tax lawyer with a Liechtenstein holding company and a client list of industrialists. From this meeting forward he is also a man the Church can telephone. The IOR business proper will not start for another fourteen years. The year is on the record and so is the name of the priest who made the introduction. Where the two men met, and what was said in the room, is not.
suggested_refs: Monsignor Amleto Giovanni Tondini, Latinist of the Secretariat of State, who made the introduction

stops.name: New York, chosen by the Gambinos
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia, which dates to 1957 his selection by the Gambino family to help manage heroin profits. A parallel research pass placed this in 'the early 1950s' while citing the same source; the source says 1957 and 1957 is used. Coordinate is a generic lower Manhattan pin: no source names a place of meeting.
stops.campa: In 1957 the Gambino family chooses him to handle the profits of heroin. The money arrives in New York as cash and has to leave as something else: deposits, loans, shares in companies with Swiss and Liechtenstein addresses. Sindona has spent the seven years since Vaduz assembling the apparatus that does exactly this. He denies the connection to his own biographer for the rest of his life. Pressed on it, he does not argue that he was clean. He argues about the class of institution the mafia uses.
stops.quote: Come sai le mie banche italiane erano istituti di prim'ordine con soci di prim'ordine. La Banca Privata Italiana era una banca dell'aristocrazia. La mafia invece si serve sempre di istituti e professionisti di second'ordine.
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona to Nick Tosches, interview material in Power on Earth / Il mistero Sindona, cited at it.wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona', note 68
suggested_refs: Nick Tosches, Power on Earth (1986); Italian edition Il mistero Sindona, SugarCo, Milano, 1986, reissued Alet 2009

stops.name: Milan, the Banca Privata Finanziaria bought
stops.date_confidence: contested year, not resolved. Treccani: 'Nel 1960 diventò un banchiere, poiche acquisi il controllo della Banca privata.' it.wikipedia: '1961: acquistò la Banca Privata Finanziaria.' Neither gives a day. 1960 is used for ordering and the conflict is stated in the campa. Coordinate is central Milan: no source fetched gives the bank's street address, so the pin is unverified rather than wrong.
stops.campa: He buys control of the Banca Privata Finanziaria, a small Milanese house, and stops being a man who advises banks. What the bank gives him is the one thing a holding company cannot: the right to take deposits, and therefore the right to use other people's money as though it were his own. He is forty years old and holds a banking licence. The year is not settled. Treccani puts the purchase in 1960 and the Italian encyclopedic record in 1961, and nobody who wrote it down at the time wrote down the day.
suggested_refs: Banca Privata Finanziaria, later merged into the Banca Privata Italiana
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: London, Hambros and the Eurodollar
stops.date_confidence: two facts merged into one stop. Hambros Bank's backing of Sindona's expansion is attested by it.wikipedia without a date beyond 'the 1960s'; en.wikipedia dates a major Eurodollar transaction to 1964. Neither gives a month or day. Coordinate is the City of London, Bishopsgate area, not a verified street address for either transaction.
stops.campa: London backs him. Hambros Bank puts its name behind his expansion, and in 1964 he closes a major Eurodollar deal in the City, opening the offshore dollar market to a bank whose entire deposit base sits in Milan. Eurodollars are dollars held outside the United States, answerable to no central bank on earth, and a man whose method is making the same money appear in two places at once has been waiting for exactly this instrument. In the City he is the Sicilian who can move Italian money. Nobody in the City asks him anything else, and Hambros leaves its name where it is.
suggested_refs: Hambros Bank, London, correspondent and backer of the Sindona group through the 1960s

stops.name: Chicago, Continental Illinois on South LaSalle
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance by it.wikipedia, which names Continental Illinois Bank of Chicago among Sindona's backers and notes that David M. Kennedy headed it before becoming Nixon's Treasury Secretary. No year is given beyond 'the 1960s'; 1965 is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to 231 South LaSalle Street, the bank's building; an earlier pass pinned it some 450 m northeast of it.
stops.campa: Continental Illinois National Bank of Chicago, on South LaSalle Street, joins the institutions lending their standing to his expansion. Its chairman, David M. Kennedy, leaves in 1969 to serve as Richard Nixon's Secretary of the Treasury. Sindona's correspondents by the middle of the decade run Milan to London to Chicago, and the American end of them reaches into a cabinet. He is not yet fifty and holds no public office of any kind, in Italy or anywhere else.
suggested_refs: Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company, 231 South LaSalle Street, Chicago
sources: OSM/Nominatim for the LaSalle Street coordinate

stops.name: Milan, the Banca Unione bought from the Feltrinellis
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani and corroborated by Britannica; no month or day in any source fetched. Coordinate is central Milan and is not a verified address for the Banca Unione.
stops.campa: He buys the Banca Unione from the family of Giangiacomo Feltrinelli, and he buys it with the Vatican's approval. Two Milanese banks are now his. He merges them into the Banca Privata Italiana, and when the merged bank goes down six years from now it will take a decade of investigators and one dead lawyer to establish what was inside it. At the time the purchase is reported as an ordinary transfer of a small institution between respectable owners.
suggested_refs: Banca Unione, Milan, merged with the Banca Privata Finanziaria into the Banca Privata Italiana
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Rome, the Società Generale Immobiliare
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Treccani and it.wikipedia for the purchase of the Vatican-linked Società Generale Immobiliare from the IOR; the month is an ordering device with no source behind it. Coordinate is the Rome city pin, not the company's registered office.
stops.campa: He buys the Società Generale Immobiliare from the Vatican Bank. The IOR is selling, Sindona is buying, and the money for the purchase is raised on the strength of the relationship the sale itself creates. From this point the two balance sheets, the Vatican's and his, are one document read twice. He is forty-eight and controls, on paper, more Roman ground than most Roman families. The company holds land in Washington as well, where it has recently finished building the Watergate complex.
suggested_refs: Società Generale Immobiliare, builder of the Watergate complex, sold by the IOR to Sindona in 1968
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Vatican City, the Torrione di Niccolò V
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the IOR relationship to 1969 and the Holy See's use of Sindona as an investment adviser to after 1968. The pin is the canonical Vatican City coordinate already used across paul_marcinkus.journey.json and licio_gelli.journey.json and is inherited byte-identical; OSM independently places the Vatican Bank entrance at 41.9038, 12.4568, about 280 m east, and that discrepancy is recorded here rather than silently applied.
stops.campa: The Institute for the Works of Religion keeps its offices in the Torrione di Niccolò V, a round fifteenth-century tower inside the Apostolic Palace. From 1968 the Holy See uses Sindona as an adviser on its investments, and by 1969 the relationship with the IOR is a working one. What he does for it first is move Vatican money offshore, ahead of an Italian tax on share dividends. The tower stands inside the walls, where no Italian magistrate can enter and no Italian tax reaches. Paul Marcinkus, the American priest from Cicero, Illinois, who will run that bank from 1971, is already inside the institution.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion', on the Torrione di Niccolò V and the Sindona years
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

stops.name: Milan, the Bastogi raid fails
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Britannica for the failed hostile takeover of Bastogi; no month or day fetched. Coordinate is the Piazza Paolo Ferrari pin already used in paul_marcinkus.journey.json for the Milanese banking quarter, inherited byte-identical; it is the district, not Bastogi's own door.
stops.campa: He moves on Bastogi, the old Milanese holding company, in a hostile takeover, and Italian finance closes ranks against him. Mediobanca and Enrico Cuccia stand in the way. The bid fails. It is the first thing Sindona attempts that the Italian establishment simply refuses him. He borrowed to fund it, and the debt stays on his books after the refusal. Five years on, indicted and hunted and talking to a reporter from L'Espresso, he is still naming Cuccia as the hand behind everything that has been done to him.
stops.quote: Ambrosoli è una creatura di Cuccia.
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona, interviewed by Gianfranco Modolo, L'Espresso, 29 February 1976
suggested_refs: Bastogi S.p.A. and the 1971 takeover battle; Mediobanca under Enrico Cuccia

stops.name: Nassau, the Cisalpine Overseas Bank
stops.date_confidence: attested. it.wikipedia has Sindona co-founding the Cisalpine Overseas Bank in Nassau with Roberto Calvi in 1971; paul_marcinkus.journey.json independently records Marcinkus on its board from roughly 1971 to 1982. Pin inherited byte-identical from that file. No month or day is given anywhere.
stops.campa: In Nassau he sets up the Cisalpine Overseas Bank with Roberto Calvi of the Banco Ambrosiano, and Paul Marcinkus sits on its board. Three men, an offshore charter, and a bank in the Bahamas whose depositors are companies owned by one another. Of the three, one will die of cyanide in an Italian prison, one will be found hanging under a London bridge, and one will die of old age in Arizona, having declined to leave the Vatican while the warrant was live.
suggested_refs: Cisalpine Overseas Bank, Nassau, later Banco Ambrosiano Overseas Ltd
Roberto Calvi, found hanged under Blackfriars Bridge, London, 18 June 1982, having fled Rome via Venice on a passport in the name Gian Roberto Calvini: his own stop, not this traveler's
sources: paul_marcinkus.journey.json (stop 'Nassau, a bishop on an offshore board')

stops.name: Mineola, Franklin National bought
stops.date_confidence: contested year. en.wikipedia dates the Fasco International purchase of a controlling interest in Franklin National Bank to 1972; Britannica's biography dates it to 1974. Both are named encyclopedic sources and the conflict is left standing. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from paul_marcinkus.journey.json. Franklin's original 1926 headquarters was at Franklin Square; it moved to Mineola in 1960, so Mineola is the address current under Sindona's ownership.
stops.campa: Franklin National Bank, headquartered at Mineola on Long Island, is the twentieth-largest bank in the United States, and Fasco International buys control of it. Sindona pays well above the market for the shares. American regulators approve a foreign owner about whom they know almost nothing. He now holds an American deposit base, and the losses accumulating in Milan have somewhere new to go. The purchase is announced as an Italian financier's vote of confidence in American banking.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'Franklin National Bank'
paul_marcinkus.journey.json (stop 'Mineola, Long Island, the Franklin National fails')

stops.name: Rome, card number 0501
stops.date_confidence: membership number attested independently by both en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia, which give Sindona as P2 member no. 0501. The join date is NOT attested: an earlier pass carried 1974 with no source, and that date is chronologically strained, since Gelli was appointed Venerable Master only in 1975. The date here orders the segment and asserts nothing. The place is likewise unattested; the Rome pin is the lodge's nominal seat and is used for want of any recorded location.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years Michele Sindona becomes member number 0501 of Propaganda Due, the lodge Licio Gelli runs out of a textile works in Tuscany and a hotel suite in Rome. The number is on the roll. The date he signed is not. P2 is not a conspiracy he joins so much as the room where the men he already deals with keep their names off paper: bankers, generals, prefects, editors. Six years from now a raid worked from a lead out of the investigation into Sindona's own banks will pull that roll out of a company archive.
suggested_refs: licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Castiglion Fibocchi, the roll in the company archive', March 1981: the raid triggered by the Sindona investigation, which is Gelli's own stop and not this traveler's

stops.name: Milan, the crash gets a name
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by en.wikipedia, which places the stock-market and banking crisis around Sindona's group in April 1974; no day. Coordinate is the Largo Bortolo Belotti pin used in licio_gelli.journey.json for the Milanese banking quarter, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: The currency positions turn. Sindona has been speculating against the lira and carrying the losses inside his own banks, and in the spring of 1974 the losses stop being carryable. In Milan the shares of his companies fall through the floor, and the depositors come to the counters for their money, which is the one thing the whole structure was built on the assumption they would not all do at once. He is fifty-three, and has been assembling that structure for twenty-four years. The Italian press names the thing in April: il crack Sindona.
suggested_refs: The Italian financial press of spring 1974 on 'il crack Sindona'

stops.name: Milan, the Banca Privata Italiana into liquidation
stops.date_confidence: full date attested by Treccani. Coordinate is the central Milan pin used for the Banca Unione and is not a verified address.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of September the Italian authorities put the Banca Privata Italiana, the merged flagship of the Banca Privata Finanziaria and the Banca Unione, into forced liquidation. What the liquidators will find inside is not a bank that lost money in the markets but a bank that had been emptied: loans to companies existing on paper, guarantees against nothing, deposits used as though they were capital, and the same funds counted twice through Vaduz.
suggested_refs: Banca Privata Italiana, liquidazione coatta amministrativa, 24 September 1974
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Koch appoints a liquidator
stops.date_confidence: date attested by Treccani and corroborated by en.wikipedia's Ambrosoli entry; it.wikipedia names Governor Guido Carli as making the appointment. The PLACE is an inference, not an attestation: the sources say only that the Bank of Italy appointed him, and Ambrosoli himself worked in Milan. Coordinate corrected to Palazzo Koch, Via Nazionale 91 (41.8976, 12.4888 per the it.wikipedia geotag); an earlier pass pinned it about 480 m north near the Quirinale.
stops.campa: Three days later the Bank of Italy appoints a liquidator. Guido Carli, its governor, picks Giorgio Ambrosoli, a Milanese lawyer of forty on nobody's list, a monarchist with no politics anyone can use and no interest whatever in being useful. Ambrosoli takes the job knowing what it is. Five months in he writes to his wife Anna that he will pay a very high price for the appointment, that he knew it before accepting, and that he is not complaining at all.
stops.quote: Pagherò a molto caro prezzo l'incarico: lo sapevo prima di accettarlo e quindi non mi lamento affatto perché per me è stata un'occasione unica per fare qualcosa di buono per il paese [...]
stops.quote_source: Giorgio Ambrosoli, letter to his wife Anna, 25 February 1975, cited in Corrado Stajano, Un eroe borghese, Einaudi, pp. 102-3 and 149
suggested_refs: Corrado Stajano, Un eroe borghese, Einaudi, Torino, 1995
Palazzo Koch, Via Nazionale 91, Rome, seat of the Banca d'Italia
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Michele Sindona'

stops.name: Mineola, Franklin National declared insolvent
stops.date_confidence: attested by Treccani, en.wikipedia and Britannica alike. Pin inherited byte-identical from paul_marcinkus.journey.json. The thirty-million-dollar transfer to Europe on the same day is en.wikipedia's figure and belongs to Sindona personally, not to the Vatican's losses, with which an earlier pass conflated it.
stops.campa: Franklin National Bank is declared insolvent and seized: the largest bank failure in the history of the United States to that date. The Federal Reserve has been feeding it emergency money for months, first to keep it alive and then to keep the failure from spreading past Long Island. The regulators who approved a foreign owner two years ago have spent this year finding out what they approved. The American depositors are made whole out of the federal insurance fund. On the same day, Sindona moves thirty million dollars out of the country to Europe.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'Franklin National Bank', on the Federal Reserve's lender-of-last-resort intervention
paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'Mineola, Long Island, the Franklin National fails'

stops.name: Vatican City, thirty-five billion lire gone
stops.date_confidence: the sum is attested as an estimate only: en.wikipedia's 'Institute for the Works of Religion' gives Vatican losses from the 1974 Franklin failure as 'estimated by one source at 35 billion Italian lire (20 million pounds)'. No source supports the thirty-million-dollar gloss an earlier pass attached to it. The date is the day after the seizure and is an ordering device, not an accounting date. Canonical Vatican pin inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: The Institute for the Works of Religion is in it with him and comes out with a hole. One estimate of the Vatican's losses on the Franklin failure is thirty-five billion lire, some twenty million pounds. The IOR publishes no accounts and answers to no regulator outside the walls, so the figure is an estimate and remains one. Marcinkus keeps his post. Within eight years he will be doing the identical business with Roberto Calvi, and Italian magistrates will issue a warrant he answers by not leaving the city state.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion', on the 35 billion lire estimate
The 1987 Italian warrant naming Marcinkus over the Banco Ambrosiano collapse: his own stop, not this traveler's

stops.name: New York, the apartment at the Hotel Pierre
stops.date_confidence: the Hotel Pierre residence is attested by it.wikipedia for the New York years, without a start date; the Italian arrest warrant and the flight to New York are dated 1974-75 by Treccani. An earlier pass had him awaiting a contemporaneous American indictment, which is wrong by about five years: the United States indicted him over Franklin only in March 1979.
stops.campa: He keeps an apartment at the Hotel Pierre on Fifth Avenue, high above Central Park, and runs a defence out of it. Italy has indicted him for fraudulent bankruptcy and wants him extradited. The United States has not indicted him at all and will not for another four years. He lobbies. He pays lawyers and public relations men. To anyone who will listen he says the same thing, which is that his banks were sound and were destroyed by enemies. The extradition fight will run nine years.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Pierre, Fifth Avenue at 61st Street, New York

stops.name: New York, the interview with L'Espresso
stops.date_confidence: the interview's publication date, interviewer and text are attested via it.wikiquote (Gianfranco Modolo, L'Espresso, 29 February 1976). The PLACE is not: one research pass assigned the quotes to Milan, but Sindona had been resident in New York as a fugitive since 1974-75, so the Hotel Pierre pin is used and the discrepancy is recorded here rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Gianfranco Modolo puts the questions and Sindona answers at length, and what comes out is not a defence but a counter-attack. Ambrosoli, he says, was beaten in the Swiss courts by Sindona's own lawyers and denounced in Italy for misappropriation. He predicts that his trial will never take place, because a trial would produce the names of the men who actually emptied his banks. Three years from now, the liquidator he is describing is shot four times outside his own front door.
stops.quote: Sono convinto che il mio processo non si farà mai, perché altrimenti salterebbero fuori i nomi di chi ha veramente svuotato le mie banche.
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona, interviewed by Gianfranco Modolo, 'Il processo lo faccio io: a Carli', L'Espresso, 29 February 1976, as reproduced at it.wikiquote
suggested_refs: Gianfranco Modolo, 'Il processo lo faccio io: a Carli', L'Espresso, 29 February 1976

stops.name: Milan, the five point six million
stops.date_confidence: the commission and the description of its recipients are attested by en.wikipedia's Ambrosoli entry: Sindona paid 'a 5.6 million dollar commission to an American bishop and a Milanese banker', identified by Italian sources as Marcinkus and Calvi. NO source fetched gives a date for the discovery; an earlier pass asserted 1978 on its own authority. The date here places the stop inside the 1974-79 liquidation and asserts nothing more.
stops.campa: Inside the liquidation Ambrosoli finds a commission of five point six million dollars paid out by Sindona, described in the records as going to an American bishop and a Milanese banker. Italian investigators put names to the description: Paul Marcinkus and Roberto Calvi. In this document the Vatican Bank is not a victim of the Sindona group; it is a counterparty being paid. Ambrosoli files it, and begins recording his telephone calls, because the calls have started to include instructions about what he should stop looking at.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'Giorgio Ambrosoli', on the 5.6 million dollar commission

stops.name: New York, the contract on the liquidator
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION, not attestation. The Venetucci recruitment chain and the figure of about 115,000 dollars come from the background dossier alone and were not corroborated against any independently fetched source in this pass; en.wikipedia's Ambrosoli entry confirms Arico's involvement and a threatening call invoking Andreotti's name, but not the payment. The month is an ordering device. Coordinate is a generic lower Manhattan pin.
stops.campa: The arrangement is made in New York. A heroin trafficker named Robert Venetucci, who had shared a cell with the man, puts Sindona in touch with William Arico, a professional killer. The price is about one hundred and fifteen thousand dollars, part cash and part Swiss transfer. Arico is flown to Milan and told where the lawyer lives. None of this comes from Sindona's mouth. It is the reconstruction the Italian courts accept seven years later, and the corroboration reachable here covers Arico and a threatening telephone call, not the price and not the cell.
suggested_refs: William Joseph Arico, named in Montanelli and Cervi's account of the trial as the killer engaged for the Ambrosoli murder
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Giorgio Ambrosoli' (Arico and the Andreotti call)

stops.name: Milan, via Morozzo della Rocca
stops.date_confidence: date attested by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia; the address, via Morozzo della Rocca 1, is given by it.wikipedia's Ambrosoli entry, and the coordinate is that street per OSM/Nominatim. An earlier pass declared the address unconfirmable and pinned the murder about 1.2 km northeast of it. The four shots from a .357 Magnum are Montanelli and Cervi's detail. Sindona was in New York; the stop is his because the Italian courts found him the mandante.
stops.campa: Giorgio Ambrosoli comes home to via Morozzo della Rocca on the evening of the eleventh of July. He has spent the day with investigators from the United States Department of Justice, going through what he found. On the steps of his own building a man shoots him four times with a .357 Magnum and walks away. Sindona is in New York and does not need to be anywhere else. The recording Ambrosoli made of a threatening call, with a voice invoking Giulio Andreotti's name, is already with the magistrates.
suggested_refs: Corrado Stajano, Un eroe borghese, Einaudi, Torino, 1995
Michele Placido, dir., Un eroe borghese (1995), in which Omero Antonutti plays Sindona

stops.name: Vienna, the first leg of a disappearance
stops.date_confidence: month attested by it.wikipedia, which places Vienna on the route of the staged abduction in August 1979; the day is an ordering device with no source behind it.
stops.campa: He disappears from New York at the beginning of August, and the first leg of the disappearance is Vienna. There is no kidnapping. There is an itinerary, built to be reconstructed afterwards by people who will conclude that a man taken against his will could plausibly have been taken this way. He wants two things at once: to be outside American jurisdiction and unavailable for trial, and to be a victim, so that Rome and the lodge can be frightened into rescuing the bank he has been demanding they rescue for five years. From Vienna the route runs to Athens, then to Brindisi.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona', on the Vienna-Athens-Brindisi route of the staged kidnapping

stops.name: Caltanissetta, carried across the island
stops.date_confidence: month attested by it.wikipedia, which puts Caltanissetta on the Sicilian leg of the route in August 1979; the day is an ordering device. The Athens and Brindisi legs are equally attested and are omitted here only for length, not for doubt.
stops.campa: Across the middle of Sicily, under escort. He came off this island in 1946 with a law degree and a black-market fortune, and he crosses it now as cargo, handed between men who owe favours to the families in New York whose money he banked. Caltanissetta is inland, dry, and nobody's destination. The route is not chosen for speed but so that a story can be told about it afterwards, with the places in the right order. Who along it was paid to see nothing, and who simply saw nothing, is in no record reached here.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona', on the Brindisi and Caltanissetta legs

stops.name: Palermo, the official arrival
stops.date_confidence: full date attested by it.wikipedia. The organising group named there is the Gambino, Bontate and Inzerillo network; 'Mafia boss' as a gloss on Rosario Spatola's role is a fair but loose reading of that source, and is flagged rather than asserted.
stops.campa: He arrives in Palermo on the seventeenth of August. The organising is done by men of the Gambino, Bontate and Inzerillo families, the Sicilian and American ends of the same trade whose profits his banks handled from 1957. Twenty-two years of that work have bought him this: a safe house, a cover story, and a set of hosts who know exactly how much he is worth to them alive and how little he is worth to them talking. He signs letters purporting to come from his captors.
suggested_refs: The Spatola-Inzerillo-Gambino network, organisers of the 1979 disappearance

stops.name: Torretta, the villa and the leg
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance by it.wikipedia: Sindona hidden at Rosario Spatola's villa in Torretta for the two months of the staged kidnapping, with a self-arranged gunshot wound to the leg. The day is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to the comune of Torretta (Palermo) per OSM/Nominatim; an earlier pass pinned it about 6.5 km northeast, in open country.
stops.campa: He is kept in the villa of Rosario Spatola at Torretta, in the hills behind Palermo, for something over two months. To make the abduction credible he has himself shot in the leg. The surgeon Joseph Miceli Crimi is brought up from Palermo to fire the shot and then to dress the wound he has just made. A hostage who comes back unmarked and in good health will not be believed. The wound is real, the leg takes weeks to heal, and he spends those weeks in a villa in the hills waiting for it to.
suggested_refs: Joseph Miceli Crimi, the Palermo surgeon who inflicted and dressed the wound

stops.name: Arezzo, the surgeon sent to Gelli
stops.date_confidence: attested as to substance: it.wikipedia says Sindona 'mandò Miceli Crimi almeno due volte ad Arezzo per convincere Licio Gelli', and the stated purpose is pressure over the rescue of his bank, not, as an earlier pass had it, coordinating P2's part in the hoax. The date is an ordering device inside the disappearance. Arezzo coordinate confirmed correct.
stops.campa: Twice during the disappearance Sindona sends Miceli Crimi north to Arezzo, to Licio Gelli, with the same message: the lodge is to force the rescue of the Banca Privata Italiana. Gelli is the man who can reach the ministers who could order it. Nothing is ordered. Eighteen months from now the roll of nine hundred and sixty-two names will be found in this province, in a company archive at Castiglion Fibocchi, by officers working a lead out of Sindona's own file.
suggested_refs: licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Castiglion Fibocchi, the roll in the company archive', March 1981

stops.name: Manhattan, out of the telephone booth
stops.date_confidence: date attested by it.wikipedia: '16 October 1979, reappeared in a Manhattan telephone booth, surrendered.' Treccani says only 'in ottobre'; an earlier pass carried 20 October, which no source supports, and pinned the booth at Times Square, which no source supports either. Coordinate is therefore a generic Manhattan approximation and is not a located booth.
stops.campa: On the ninth of October Vincenzo Spatola is arrested in Italy delivering a letter written by a hostage who is not one. A week later Michele Sindona steps out of a telephone booth in Manhattan and hands himself back to the authorities with an account of left-wing terrorists and a bullet wound to show for it. The account does not survive the first questions. He has been gone seventy-five days, no bank has been rescued, whatever credit he had left with the Church and the lodge is gone, and the leg is healing.
suggested_refs: The arrest of Vincenzo Spatola, 9 October 1979, carrying the fabricated letter from captivity

stops.name: Foley Square, sixty-five counts
stops.date_confidence: the conviction on 65 counts and the sentence of 25 years with a 207,000 dollar fine are attested by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia; the year is firm, the month of March comes from the background dossier and could not be independently pinned in this pass, so the day defaults to 01. The two suicide attempts by wrist-cutting are it.wikipedia's and the dossier's and are tagged as reconstruction in the report.
stops.campa: In the federal courthouse at Foley Square a Manhattan jury convicts him on sixty-five counts: fraud, perjury, misappropriation of bank funds, false statements, all of it arising out of Franklin National. He is sentenced to twenty-five years and fined two hundred and seven thousand dollars. Twice in the course of the proceedings he cuts his wrists. The American case is finished inside a year. No source reached here names the federal prison that holds him for the four years after it.
suggested_refs: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, Foley Square

stops.name: Foley Square, the second verdict
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION. This conviction is carried by the background dossier alone. The full en.wikipedia article contains no sentence dated 1981, and it.wikipedia records only the 1980 American conviction and the 1985-86 Italian ones. Perjury already sits among the 65 counts of 1980, so the 1981 trial may be a duplication of the same case. The five-hour deliberation is likewise dossier-only. One research lens tagged this attested and another reconstruction; the lower tag is used.
stops.campa: He is tried again in the same courthouse, on charges of jumping bail and lying under oath about the disappearance, and convicted. The account of it says the jury took five hours. Whether this is a separate case at all is not clear from the reference record: perjury already sits among the sixty-five counts of 1980, and the standard articles carry no 1981 verdict at all. It is set down here as it was found, on the authority of one dossier and no archive.
suggested_refs: Any Southern District of New York docket for an April 1981 bail-jumping and perjury trial, which would settle whether this is a distinct case

stops.name: Voghera, extradited to the prison on via Ambrosoli
stops.date_confidence: full date attested by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia; Treccani gives only September 1984. Coordinate corrected to the Casa Circondariale di Voghera per OSM/Nominatim, which records its address as Via Giorgio Ambrosoli; an earlier pass pinned it about 2 km northeast, missing even the town.
stops.campa: Extradited at last, he lands in Italy and is taken to the maximum-security prison at Voghera, on the Lombard plain south of Pavia. The street the prison stands on is called via Giorgio Ambrosoli. He is sixty-four. Ten years have gone since the Banca Privata Italiana was put into liquidation, and he has spent every one of them arguing that he was the victim of the affair rather than its author. The Italian courts will take eighteen months to finish with him.
suggested_refs: Casa Circondariale di Voghera, Via Giorgio Ambrosoli, Cascina Ridondello

stops.name: Milan, the Palazzo di Giustizia on the bankruptcy
stops.date_confidence: contested sentence length, not resolved. Both en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia give 16 March 1985 and twelve years for the fraudulent bankruptcy of the Banca Privata Italiana; Treccani gives fifteen years and no day. Two sources to one, and only the sources carrying a day carry twelve, so twelve leads and Treccani is footnoted here. Coordinate corrected to the Palazzo di Giustizia, Via Freguglia 1, per OSM; an earlier pass pinned it about 1.1 km west.
stops.campa: A Milan court convicts him of the fraudulent bankruptcy of the Banca Privata Italiana on the sixteenth of March. The sentence is twelve years, or fifteen: the reference works disagree, and the ones that give a day give twelve. Eleven years have passed since the collapse. What the court establishes is what Giorgio Ambrosoli had established in his first year of work, and Ambrosoli has been dead for six. The other case, the one about how he came to be dead, is still to be tried in the same building.
suggested_refs: Tribunale di Milano, Palazzo di Giustizia, Via Freguglia 1
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (fifteen years)

stops.name: Milan, l'ergastolo
stops.date_confidence: full date attested by Treccani, en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia. Note that the Montanelli and Cervi passage quoted here dates the Ambrosoli murder to 12 July 1979 while the encyclopedic record gives 11 July; the quote is reproduced verbatim and the discrepancy is left standing in it. Courthouse coordinate corrected as at the 1985 stop.
stops.campa: The Corte d'Assise of Milan finds Michele Sindona guilty of aggravated homicide as the man who ordered the killing of Giorgio Ambrosoli, and sentences him to life. He is sixty-five. Montanelli and Cervi will write that the bankruptcy made him a protagonist and that after July of 1979 he was something a great deal worse than that. The verdict is read out. He is driven back to Voghera the same day, sixty kilometres south, and the appeal his lawyers plan will never be argued.
stops.quote: Protagonista di una bancarotta, Sindona fu, dopo il 12 luglio 1979, qualcosa di molto peggio: mandante d'un omicidio... la Corte d'Assise di Milano dichiarò Michele Sindona colpevole di omicidio aggravato e lo condannò all'ergastolo.
stops.quote_source: Indro Montanelli and Mario Cervi, L'Italia degli anni di fango (1978-1993), p. 195
suggested_refs: Indro Montanelli e Mario Cervi, L'Italia degli anni di fango (1978-1993), Rizzoli

stops.name: Voghera, the coffee in the bathroom
stops.date_confidence: date attested by it.wikipedia: 20 March 1986, potassium cyanide in prison coffee, two days after the life sentence. Two earlier passes dated the poisoning 18 March, the day of the verdict, while their own prose said 'two days after' it; the internal contradiction is resolved here to the 20th on the source's authority. The exclamation is real but its attribution had to be corrected: it is not traceable to Simoni and Turone, and is reported in la Repubblica's judicial reconstruction of 4 November 1986. Prison coordinate corrected as at the 1984 stop.
stops.campa: On the morning of the twentieth of March he carries his coffee into the bathroom to sugar it, out of sight of the guards. When he comes back out to the officers he shouts that he has been poisoned. He shouts it twice. It is potassium cyanide, a massive dose, and it is in him by half past eight, two days after the life sentence. Eighteen months earlier a financial columnist had written that Sindona lived in terror of one day being served a coffee alla Pisciotta.
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona, Voghera prison, morning of 20 March 1986; judicial reconstruction reported in la Repubblica, 'Ecco gli ultimi istanti di Sindona', 4 November 1986
suggested_refs: Alberto Mazzuca, Il Sole 24 Ore, 30 September 1984: 'È pensabile che Sindona, il quale vive nel terrore di ricevere prima o poi un caffè alla Pisciotta, si metta ora a raccontare qualche particolare inedito solo per porre in difficoltà qualcuno dei suoi più vecchi e altolocati amici?'
Gianni Simoni and Giuliano Turone, Il caffè di Sindona, Garzanti, 2009
sources: la Repubblica archive, 'Ecco gli ultimi istanti di Sindona', 4 November 1986

stops.name: Voghera, the civil hospital
stops.date_confidence: death on 22 March 1986 at Voghera, aged 65, attested by Treccani and both Wikipedias. Two disputes recorded rather than resolved: one research pass placed the death in the hospital OF the maximum-security prison, while it.wikipedia says the Voghera hospital, which is followed here; and the widely repeated '53 hours on life support' appears in no fetched source, it.wikipedia saying only a two-day coma. Coordinate is the Ospedale Civile di Voghera per OSM/Nominatim.
stops.campa: He is carried to the civil hospital at Voghera and does not regain consciousness. Two days later, on the twenty-second of March, he is declared dead at sixty-five. The ruling is suicide. Treccani puts it harder than that and says he killed himself with cyanide while staging a murder, which would make the last operation of his life the same operation as the kidnapping: a real injury arranged to produce a false story. How potassium cyanide got inside a maximum-security prison has never been answered.
suggested_refs: Ospedale Civile di Voghera
Treccani's formulation: 'si suicidò con il cianuro... simulando un omicidio'

stops.name: Cimitero Monumentale, tomb 430
stops.date_confidence: burial site and plot attested by it.wikipedia: Cimitero Monumentale di Milano, tomb 430, Circondario di Levante. No source gives the date of burial; 26 March is an ordering device only. Coordinate is the cemetery per OSM; two earlier passes gave two different values for the same tomb, 45.4839/9.1793 and 45.4858/9.1791, the first of which falls outside the cemetery walls.
stops.campa: He is buried in Milan, in the Cimitero Monumentale, tomb 430 of the Circondario di Levante, in the city where he opened a law office in 1946 and where the bank he emptied was wound up in 1974. Ambrosoli lies in the same city. The tomb is a family tomb and carries the family name; nothing on it records the Franklin National Bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion, or the lodge. Within ten years the case has a film. It is called Un eroe borghese, Michele Placido directs it, the hero is the murdered liquidator, and Omero Antonutti plays Sindona.
suggested_refs: Michele Placido, dir., Un eroe borghese (1995), David di Donatello for Best Producer and a special David for civil and artistic value
Qualunque cosa succeda. Giorgio Ambrosoli, una storia vera (RAI, 2014), with Pierfrancesco Favino as Ambrosoli
